answers.answer: Choose the table by time scope. For current-stream information, use the Live now helpers, such as {stream.game}, {stream.title}, {stream.uptime} and {stream.viewers}. For a historical result, use the Counts and top lists helpers, which read the newest recorded stream and keep that stream after you end it. You can also use the {stream.last.*} helpers, which read the newest stream that has ended. Arguments go after a colon: {stream.title.short:N} takes 1 to 140, and {stream.games.history:N} and {stream.topChatters:N} take 1 to 25.
answers.quote: Live now reads the channel as it is at this moment.

answers.answer: You need a reply field that takes templates. The Use in column lists which fields accept each helper. For text a viewer writes, the Viewer Templates setting and permissions also apply. The bot must have recorded a stream before the count and last-stream helpers give a value. All of this is in the opening paragraphs.
answers.quote: Type one in any reply field that takes templates, and the bot fills it in when it sends the message.

answers.answer: When it works, the helper is replaced by a value like the one in the Example column. When it does not, the helper text stays in the message as typed. That happens when no stream is recorded, a number is missing, or a Live now form is used while offline. The concepts differ by which stream they read: the live channel, the newest recorded stream, or the newest ended stream.
answers.quote: A helper with no value stays in the message as you typed it.

answers.answer: The command about the current game uses {stream.game}, which reads the live channel now. A recap posted while live that needs the previous stream's totals uses the {stream.last.*} helpers, because while live the count helpers describe the running stream. A recap posted right after ending the stream can use the count helpers, because they still describe the stream that just ended.
answers.quote: For a recap you post while live, use these. For one you post right after you end the stream, the count helpers above already describe that stream and carry more detail.

answers.answer: I reread {stream.topChatters}: it accepts 1 to 25 but returns five names at most. The opening paragraphs explain the five-name cap, so I could go on, but I had to check that 25 is not a typo. The cost is one reread.
answers.quote: give how many, from 1 to 25, after a colon, and you get five names at most. With no number it stays as typed

answers.answer: Read aloud, the long example links in the Live now table (box art, directory and preview picture) are hard to follow. {stream.raids.lastRaider} is described as the biggest raid, not the latest one, so a listener could be thrown by the name. Both cost a moment of attention but block no task.
answers.quote: The channel that raided with the most viewers

warning_review.reason: The five short sentences each carry one idea: the helper prefix, the reply fields that accept it, what the live-channel helpers read, the recap case, and the rule that the table decides which stream a helper reads. This is the scope statement the reader needs before the tables, and the count alone is not a defect.

Each of the five sentences gives a separate fact the reader needs: the no-value rule, when it happens, the thousands separator, the banned-viewer exclusion that changes counts, and the last-stream exception that counts every viewer. The banned-viewer difference changes what a count means, so the length costs less than a missing rule.
